newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi lists costs of new watershed pact.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi lists costs of new watershed pact.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi, who had held up a $2.2 billion pact to protect the city's drinking water while he sought improvements, on Tuesday unveiled a list of the plan's costs.

Hevesi who estimated the program would cost the city about $2.2 billion, noted the new pact that he agreed still was not fail-safe, and raised concerns about how all the money will be spent that showed the potential for problems in balancing the city's interests with those of upstate areas.

"That (cost) includes appropriate expenses, such as improving sewage treatment, and questionable costs, such as paying attorneys to defend the towns if the city challenges how much they raise taxes on land the city owns or buys," he said in prepared remarks.

"If the Memorandum of Agreement protects the city's water, allows the city to avoid the much higher costs of filtration and leads to a cooperative relationship with upstate communities, it will have been a good investment. If the agreement fails, it will have been money down the drain."

The federal Environmental Protection Agency in 1993 gave the city three years to act on a plan to protect its drinking water from development in the watershed area or build a new filtration plant that was estimated to cost $5 billion.

The city opted to agree a plan to protect the 19 reservoirs that provide almost 9 million residents in the city and Westchester County with 1.5 billion gallons of water a day. It aims to safeguard the city's drinking water in part by buying land around its reservoirs in upstate communities to protect it from development while still allowing the areas to grow.
The plan's costs, which were listed by the city comptroller, follow:
--Interest on debt to finance the pact, $570 million.

--Other unknown costs, $200 million. These items were listed as additional operating and maintenance costs of all existing and future sewage treatment plants in the watershed that are needed to comply with city regulations.
